WHAT THE CLASS IS. A typeset subscript digit that OCR flattened into a comma or a lookalike letter. Live on user-facing surfaces until now: "Vitamin B,," for B12 (14 times), "Vitamin B," for B3/B6, "(B,)" for (B6), "LDso"/"LDSO" for LD50, "Vitamin 81" for Vitamin B1. A destroyed vitamin number is not cosmetic -- it is the identity of the nutrient the reader is being told about. THE AMBIGUITY THAT MADE THIS A READING JOB RATHER THAN A RULE. A comma in "B,," can be TWO destroyed digits, or ONE digit plus a real comma. Both shapes are live in the same book: "Vitamin B,, discovered in 1879 and isolated in 1932, is a key cofactor" resolves to "Vitamin B2," -- subscript 2 plus a genuine appositive comma -- while "the primary forms of B,, are methylcobalamin" resolves to "B12", two digits and no comma.   ↳ Two things this pass. Six more broken quotes are fixed — including the last defect in the pregnancy anecdote Luneth first reported, which now reads correctly end to end. And the five detector classes turned out to sit on top of a bigger problem that I could not measure, which matters more than the six fixes. THE FINDING. Our text says "magnesium at2,000 mg". The page says "magnesium at 2,000 mg" — with a space. Same story for "zinc at 5-15 mg b.i.d." (we had zincat5-15mgb.i.d.) and "fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d." (we had 5gmt.i.d.). Let's Play Doctor is tightly JUSTIFIED: the typesetter squeezed the thin spaces to make lines fit, and the OCR dropped them entirely. On those same pages I can read "andelectrolytes", "ratherthan", "allthree" — all letter-to-letter, and therefore invisible to every one of the five detectors, which only ever see the letter-to-digit and camelCase EDGES of that class. I TRIED TO MEASURE HOW BIG IT IS AND MY MEASUREMENT WAS INVALID. I wrote a vocabulary detector — a token that is not a word but splits cleanly into two words — and it returned 387 candidates across 326 claims. Almost every one was a legitimate word the speller simply does not know: cofactor, peroxidation, subluxations, anticarcinogenic, Framingham, Reichstein, epigenetics. It was the same trap as the lowercase_line_start detector I threw away earlier today, which flagged 69% of the corpus because a verbatim is a mid-sentence slice of wrapped prose. So the honest position is: the dropped-space class is REAL, confirmed by eye on three separate pages, and of UNKNOWN size. Publishing a number would be worse than publishing none, because the number would be wrong and would be quoted back later as if it were measured. The consequence is the part to carry forward. Promoting the five classes to gates does not make the corpus clean of dropped spaces. It makes it clean of the EDGES of that class. That is still worth doing — an edge caught is a defect caught — but it has to be stated plainly, or a green board will imply a cleanliness nobody established. This is the same shape as the limit already written into frontface_verbatims_clean: a mechanical gate holds a floor, it does not certify a page. The converse is the load-bearing caveat: a KEEP verdict is NEGATIVE evidence and is only as good as its input.
